title: Three States, Three Bypolls: Counting Day Looms for Bankipur, Datia, Manjalpur
excerpt: Vote counting on August 3 will decide the fate of Prashant Kishor's electoral debut in Bihar's Bankipur, BJP's contested pick in Datia, and a legacy battle in Gujarat's Manjalpur.
body:
• Vote counting for bypolls in Bankipur (Bihar), Datia (Madhya Pradesh), and Manjalpur (Gujarat) is scheduled for August 3, with results expected the same day.
  • Bankipur is the marquee contest: Jan Suraj founder Prashant Kishor is making his electoral debut against BJP's Neeraj Kumar Sinha in a seat the party has held for decades.
  • Voter turnout varied widely — Datia recorded 71.4%, while Bankipur and Manjalpur saw lower figures of 34.3% and 37.5% respectively.

Three assembly seats across Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat go to counting on August 3 after voting concluded on July 30. Each contest carries its own political subplot, but the one drawing national attention is Bankipur — where election strategist-turned-politician Prashant Kishor is testing whether his campaign playbook works when he's the candidate.

Bankipur: Kishor's First Test at the Ballot Box

The Bankipur seat in Patna became vacant after BJP national president Nitin Nabin resigned as MLA following his elevation to the Rajya Sabha in April. Nabin had held the constituency since 2010, making it a BJP stronghold in the heart of Bihar's capital.

Kishor, founder of the Jan Suraj Party, chose this seat for his electoral debut — a deliberate challenge to the BJP on its home turf. He framed the contest as a "referendum" on the NDA government's performance in Bihar.

"We view this as the beginning of a new kind of politics in Bihar. It is not anyone's stronghold; it is the stronghold of the people of Bihar."

— Prashant Kishor, Jan Suraj Party founder

The BJP fielded Neeraj Kumar Sinha, while the RJD nominated Rekha Gupta, setting up a three-way race. Voting day was marred by an incident at Polling Booth No. 141 on Daldali Road, where a shot was fired, leaving a bullet mark on a window. Turnout was sluggish — just 34.3% by the close of polls, well below the 2025 assembly election pace, according to Dainik Bhaskar.

Datia: BJP's Candidate Swap Stirs Internal Tensions

In Madhya Pradesh's Datia, the bypoll was triggered by the disqualification of Congress MLA Rajendra Bharti in April following his conviction in a bank fraud case under Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act. Bharti had defeated former BJP Home Minister Narottam Mishra from the seat in the 2023 assembly elections.

The BJP was widely expected to field Mishra to reclaim the constituency. Instead, the party nominated first-time candidate Ashutosh Tiwari — a decision that sparked protests from Mishra's supporters. Several party workers were booked on allegations of attacking government officials and vandalism. Mishra, visibly emotional when Tiwari's candidacy was announced on July 13, eventually appealed to his supporters to rally behind the party's choice.

Congress fielded veteran Kunwar Ghanshyam Singh, contesting for the seventh time. Internal rifts surfaced there too, with disqualified MLA Bharti reportedly pushing for a family member to get the ticket. Datia recorded the highest turnout of the three seats at 71.4%.

Manjalpur: Carrying Forward a Legacy

The Manjalpur seat in Vadodara, Gujarat, fell vacant after the death of eight-time BJP MLA Yogesh Patel on June 2. Patel had represented the constituency since 1990 and served as the Assembly's Pro-tem Speaker and a Minister of State.

The BJP nominated Satish Patel, a former Vadodara district party president with deep roots in cooperative politics. Congress put up veteran leader Bhikhabhai Rabari, 79, a former state minister and Gujarat Congress vice-president who campaigned on civic issues — poor roads, water quality, and drainage problems in Vadodara.

Manjalpur is considered a safe BJP seat, but dissatisfaction among local leaders over the candidate prompted the party to deploy a roster of senior figures — including union ministers, the chief minister, and the state party president — during the campaign. Turnout came in at 37.5%.

What's Next

Counting begins on August 3, with results expected the same day. The Election Commission has said the entire election process will be completed by August 4.

For the BJP, all three seats offer the chance to consolidate. Bankipur and Manjalpur were already party-held, while Datia was a Congress seat won amid unusual circumstances. For Kishor, a credible showing in Bankipur — even short of victory — could validate Jan Suraj as a political force ahead of Bihar's next assembly elections. A loss in a low-turnout contest, however, would raise questions about whether the strategist's grassroots appeal can match his campaign acumen.

For the Indian diaspora watching Bihar politics, the Bankipur result is a barometer: Kishor has explicitly pitched his movement as post-caste, post-dynasty politics — the kind of reform NRIs have long called for. Whether voters agree will be clear on Monday.
